findings.where: Screen 2 (One current: field, torque, speed), the words above and below the picture
findings.what: This SHOW screen carries about 126 words of prose plus a 53-word worked box, well over 90: a 14-word task, a 58-word assumptions paragraph and a live caption of up to 55 words. The paragraph and the caption say the same two things (field follows current so torque goes with current squared; weaker field so faster), so keep only the assumption and the example-line label above the picture and let the caption carry the cause.

findings.where: Screen 2 assumptions paragraph and live caption; screen 3 Why ("A weaker field must spin faster to make the same back-emf")
findings.what: The sentence says the field spins, but the field winding is stationary and the armature spins. Write "In a weaker field the armature must spin faster to make the same back-emf."

No screen says why the back-emf must stay the same. It settles just under the supply voltage (E = V − I R, nearly V once resistance is ignored), so a weaker field needs more speed. Without that step "speed goes with one over the current" is asserted, not explained, and E = V − I R first appears on the Keep this card.

No screen gives the step behind current squared: torque is the field times the armature current, and here both are the one current. Screen 1 jumps to "a stronger field and much more torque" and screen 2 to "The field grows with the current. So torque goes with current squared". The explain text has the step ("Torque comes from the field acting on the armature current. Here both are that one current."), but the screens do not.

The two texts carry 13 footnote marks, against the rule of a few per lesson, each on a figure he would look up on a job. [^11] sits on the series-connection definition he already knows and [^1] on "no back-emf at standstill". Keep the starting-current figures ([^4], [^9], [^10]) and drop the rest.

The stem already names the cause ("The belt snaps, and the motor races"), so picking "The belt drive" needs no thought. It also tests the same idea as screen 3. Either give only the symptom (a belt-driven fan motor suddenly races and trips on overspeed) or make the fault to find the lesson's other named slip: the supply leads were swapped and it still turns the same way.

The drawing shows field, torque and speed but not the back-emf that drives the speed rise. A back-emf bar that stays level while the field bar shrinks and the armature speeds up would draw the cause. The hoist's load box also stays the same size while he drags the load current down.
The slider stops at full load, so the very high starting torque is never seen. Running it to 2.00 would show the lesson's own "double the current, four times the torque" (torque 4.00, speed 0.50).
"0.25 × 0.25 = 0.06" is 0.0625 rounded. Write "= 0.0625, about 0.06" so a hand check matches.

findings.where: Keep this card, rule lines; screen 4 Starting current row
findings.what: R in "E = V − I R" and "I = V ÷ R" is never defined. For a series motor R is the armature plus the series field, but 260 ÷ 0.4 uses the armature's 0.4 Ω alone. Say in one short line that the field's resistance makes the real figure a little less; the practice text already says so.

findings.where: Keep this card, rule and notes
findings.what: "Below saturation, ignoring resistance: torque goes with I²" ties the torque rule to ignoring resistance, but only the speed rule needs that. "A starting resistance limits the start" should say "limits the starting current", and the two ranges (125 to 200% and two to three times) need a closing line such as "Use the maker's setting."

findings.where: Keep this card, What it is for and Where it lives
findings.what: The two sections say nearly the same words ("loads that need big starting torque and stay coupled"), and the Where line runs two colons together. Let Where it lives just list the uses.

The only marine line is a 1907 US Navy boat-crane record. It tells Dan nothing about a modern ship, and research itself calls it old practice (they thought gear losses would stop racing). Present it plainly as history or drop it.

The lesson starts from the AC circuits generator idea, not from a series motor he has used. His sheet lists grinders, and research holds universal-motor notes. If a source ties grinders to the universal motor, one line ("the motor in a grinder is a series motor built to run on AC too") would anchor the lesson in kit he knows.
The three readouts sit two then one, which leaves Speed alone on half a row. Stack them, or keep all three on one row.
